# Modules and namespaces

[Glyph index](glyphs.qmd)

A BPL file that [`•load`](system/load.qmd) runs is a module. A module has names of its own. `•load` returns a record of the module's public names, and adds no names to the code that loads it.

```bpl
n←•load "lib/numeric.bpl"
n.factors 360              ⍝ 2 2 2 3 3 5
```

BPL's modules follow BQN's [namespaces](https://mlochbaum.github.io/BQN/doc/namespace.html). In BQN, a namespace is a kind of value of its own. In BPL, `•load` returns an ordinary record.

## Taking names

To take names from the record, destructure it by key, as in `[factors: factorial:]`. Each name is assigned the item with the same key. Names the pattern doesn't mention stay in the record. [Assignment](assignment.ipynb#destructuring) covers patterns.

```bpl
[factors: factorial:]←•load "lib/numeric.bpl"
factorial 5                ⍝ 120
```

A record holds operators as well as functions and arrays. Read an operator from a record with a dot path or by destructuring.

```bpl
a←•load "lib/array.bpl"
10 -a.foldl 1 2 3          ⍝ 4
[foldl:]←a
10 -foldl 1 2 3            ⍝ 4
```

Each `•load` runs the file again and returns a new record. Load a file again after you edit it to get the new version.

## Records as namespaces

Any record also works as a namespace. Inside `T.(expr)`, each key of `T` is a name for its item:

```bpl
order←["price":2 3 5;"qty":10 20 1]
order.(+/price×qty)            ⍝ 85
```

Names that aren't keys come from the code around the expression. A key hides an outer name with the same spelling.

```bpl
order←["price":2 3 5;"qty":10 20 1]
rate←0.5 ◇ order.(price×≥rate)    ⍝ 3 4.5 7.5
```

A dfn's argument, operand and recursion names, `α ω ⍶ ⍹ ∇ ⍢`, are the exception. They always come from the call, even when a key has the same spelling:

```bpl
f←{["ω":0].(ω+1)} ◇ f 5        ⍝ 6
```

An assignment inside the parentheses is local to the expression, as an assignment in a dfn is local to the dfn. To change a field, assign to its dot path, as in `order.qty←5 5 5`.

```bpl
order←["price":2 3 5;"qty":10 20 1]
r←order.(qty←0) ◇ order.qty    ⍝ 10 20 1
```

`T⍎text` evaluates the code in `text` with the keys of `T` as names, like Dyalog's `ns⍎text`:

```bpl
order←["price":2 3 5;"qty":10 20 1]
order⍎"+/price×qty"            ⍝ 85
```

Because a key that holds a function binds as a function, a module's record works as a namespace too:

```bpl
n←•load "lib/numeric.bpl"
n.(factors 360)                ⍝ 2 2 2 3 3 5
```

An array with keys on its first axis also works as a namespace. Each key names its major cell, which in a matrix is a row:

```bpl
prices←"cost" "sale":[2 3 5◇4 4 9]
prices.(sale-cost)             ⍝ 2 1 4
```

`T.(expr)` uses one array as its namespace. For an array of records, `{ω.(expr)}¨records` evaluates `expr` in each record.

## Writing a module

A module is a file of BPL statements, run in order each time it's loaded. Loading a module doesn't display the results of its statements, but explicit `⎕←` output appears. Every name assigned at the top level is public, except a name that starts with `_`. A private name is left out of the record. The module's own functions can still use it.

```text
⍝ stats.bpl
_sq←{ω×ω}
mean←+/÷≢
var←{mean _sq ω-mean ω}
```

`•load "stats.bpl"` returns a record that holds `mean` and `var`. `var` still uses `_sq` when you call it.

## Modules that use other modules

A path that starts with `./` or `../` is relative to the file that holds the code. A module finds the files beside it this way, whatever the working directory is. Other relative paths are relative to the working directory. [`•nget`](system/nget.qmd) and `•nput` follow the same rule. A module reads a data file beside it with `•nget "./table.csv"`.

A module that uses another module usually keeps it under a private name, which keeps the other module's names out of its record:

```text
⍝ report.bpl
_stats←•load "./stats.bpl"
summary←{[_stats.mean ω;_stats.var ω]}
```

To export the other module, give it a public name. With `stats←•load "./stats.bpl"`, the record of `report.bpl` would hold the `stats` record too. Destructured names are public as well: `[mean:]←•load "./stats.bpl"` makes `mean` one of the module's names.

Loading a file that loads itself, directly or through other files, raises a `DOMAIN` error.

## The library

The files in `lib/` are modules. They load each other with `./` paths and private names: `lib/graph.bpl` holds `lib/array.bpl` as `_array`, and uses `_array.dsp`.

## Names in the session

The names of a loaded module aren't session names. `]names` and name completion don't list them. Take the names you use, or keep the record and use dot paths.

From Python, `bpl('•load "lib/array.bpl"').py` gives the record as a dict. Its functions are `Function` objects. Its operators are `Operator` objects, which you call with their operands to get a function:

```python
from basedpl import bpl
a = bpl('•load "lib/array.bpl"').py
a['foldl'](bpl.fn('-'))(10, [1, 2, 3]).py   # 4
```
